## 1. Overview

This guide defines the end-to-end development workflow for the Predictive Braking System project. It covers the architectural phases from initial requirements through production deployment, the theoretical underpinning of the braking model, a systematic debugging strategy, and the conventions that govern how code, branches, and commits are managed across the repository.

This document is intended for:

- **New contributors** onboarding to the project
- **AI coding assistants** (Cursor, Copilot, Gemini) used as pair-programming tools
- **Reviewers** auditing implementation decisions against the original design intent

---

## 2. Architecture Phases

The project follows a five-phase lifecycle. Each phase has a defined entry criterion, set of deliverables, and an exit criterion before the next phase begins.

---

### Phase 1 — Foundation & Requirements

**Goal:** Establish a shared, unambiguous understanding of the problem domain before a single line of code is written.

| Activity | Owner | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Domain research & literature review | Lead Engineer | `docs/research/references.md` |
| Requirements elicitation (stakeholder interviews) | PM / Lead | `docs/requirements/PRD.md` |
| Sensor & data-source inventory | Hardware Team | `docs/hardware/sensor_map.md` |
| Constraint definition (latency, safety margins) | Systems Architect | `docs/architecture/constraints.md` |
| Glossary alignment | All | `docs/GLOSSARY.md` |

**Entry Criterion:** Project charter approved.  
**Exit Criterion:** PRD signed off, constraints document reviewed by safety team.

---

### Phase 2 — Core Algorithm Development

**Goal:** Implement and validate the predictive braking model in an isolated, testable environment.

| Activity | Owner | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Mathematical model prototyping | Algorithm Team | `src/core/braking_model.py` |
| Physics simulation harness | QA / Algorithm | `tests/simulation/` |
| Parameter sweep & sensitivity analysis | Data Scientist | `notebooks/param_sweep.ipynb` |
| Unit test suite (>90% coverage) | QA | `tests/unit/` |
| Algorithm design document | Lead Engineer | `docs/architecture/algorithm_design.md` |

**Key Inputs:** Sensor map, constraint document, physics constants.  
**Exit Criterion:** Model achieves target stopping-distance accuracy across all simulation scenarios defined in the PRD.

---

### Phase 3 — Integration & Middleware

**Goal:** Connect the validated algorithm to real sensor feeds, vehicle CAN bus, and the actuation layer.

| Activity | Owner | Output |
|---|---|---|
| CAN bus interface implementation | Embedded Team | `src/middleware/can_interface.py` |
| Sensor fusion module | Algorithm + Embedded | `src/middleware/sensor_fusion.py` |
| Real-time scheduler integration | Systems Architect | `src/middleware/scheduler.py` |
| End-to-end integration tests | QA | `tests/integration/` |
| Latency profiling baseline | Performance Eng. | `docs/performance/latency_baseline.md` |

**Entry Criterion:** Phase 2 exit criteria met, hardware test rig available.  
**Exit Criterion:** Integration tests pass on hardware rig at ≥99.5% reliability; latency within spec.

---

### Phase 4 — Testing & Validation

**Goal:** Prove system correctness, safety, and resilience across the full operational envelope.

| Activity | Owner | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing | QA + Hardware | `tests/hil/` |
| Edge-case & fault-injection testing | QA | `tests/fault_injection/` |
| Safety-critical path review | Safety Engineer | `docs/safety/safety_review.md` |
| Regression suite baseline | QA | `tests/regression/` |
| Performance benchmarking | Performance Eng. | `docs/performance/benchmark_results.md` |

**Entry Criterion:** Phase 3 exit criteria met, safety review scheduled.  
**Exit Criterion:** All safety-critical paths verified, zero P0 defects open, benchmark results within spec.

---

### Phase 5 — Deployment & Monitoring

**Goal:** Ship to production and maintain observability, correctness, and rapid incident response.

| Activity | Owner | Output |
|---|---|---|
| CI/CD pipeline configuration | DevOps | `.github/workflows/` |
| Production deployment playbook | DevOps | `docs/ops/deployment_playbook.md` |
| Telemetry & alerting setup | SRE | `docs/ops/monitoring.md` |
| On-call runbook | SRE | `docs/ops/runbook.md` |
| Post-deployment smoke tests | QA | `tests/smoke/` |

**Entry Criterion:** Phase 4 exit criteria met, deployment playbook reviewed.  
**Exit Criterion:** System live, dashboards green, on-call rotation established.

---

## 3. Predictive Braking Theory

### 3.1 Problem Statement

Standard reactive braking responds to a hazard only after it is detected. Predictive braking aims to **anticipate** the need to decelerate by fusing forward-looking sensor data with a physics-based model, reducing stopping distance and improving passenger safety.

### 3.2 Core Physics Model

The fundamental relationship governing vehicle stopping distance is:

```
d_stop = v² / (2 · μ · g)
```

Where:
- `d_stop` — minimum stopping distance (meters)
- `v` — current vehicle velocity (m/s)
- `μ` — road-surface friction coefficient (dimensionless, estimated from sensor fusion)
- `g` — gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s²)

### 3.3 Predictive Distance Horizon

The system maintains a **threat horizon** — a forward-looking distance computed as:

```
d_horizon = v · t_reaction + d_stop + d_margin
```

Where:
- `t_reaction` — system actuation latency (measured in Phase 3 profiling)
- `d_margin` — configurable safety buffer (default: 2.5 m, tunable via `config/safety_params.yaml`)

Any detected object or predicted hazard entering `d_horizon` triggers the braking pipeline.

### 3.4 Friction Coefficient Estimation

`μ` is not directly measurable in real time. The system uses a **Kalman-filtered fusion** of:

1. **Wheel slip ratio** — derived from wheel-speed sensors vs. vehicle speed
2. **Longitudinal acceleration** — from the IMU
3. **Road condition classifier** — a lightweight ML model trained on camera + LIDAR features (`src/ml/road_classifier.py`)

The fused estimate updates at 100 Hz. Historical estimates feed a rolling window (configurable, default 2 s) to smooth transient spikes.

### 3.5 Threat Classification

Detected objects are scored by a **Threat Priority Index (TPI)**:

```
TPI = (v_relative / d_object) · w_object_class · w_trajectory
```

Where:
- `v_relative` — closing speed (m/s)
- `d_object` — current distance to object (m)
- `w_object_class` — class weight (pedestrian = 1.0, cyclist = 0.9, vehicle = 0.8, static = 0.5)
- `w_trajectory` — trajectory overlap score with ego path [0, 1]

Objects with `TPI > TPI_THRESHOLD` (configurable) are escalated to the braking actuator.

### 3.6 Actuator Command Generation

The braking command is computed as:

```
a_cmd = -min(a_max, v² / (2 · d_available))
```

Where:
- `a_max` — maximum safe deceleration (configurable, default: −8.5 m/s²)
- `d_available` — distance to the nearest high-TPI object minus `d_margin`

The command is rate-limited to prevent jerky actuation (jerk limit configurable in `config/actuation_params.yaml`).

---

## 4. Debugging Strategy

The project uses a **layered debugging protocol**: start at the highest abstraction, narrow to the lowest only as needed. This prevents over-diving into embedded C when a configuration YAML is the actual culprit.

### 4.1 Layer 0 — Configuration Verification

Before touching code, verify:

```bash
# Validate all config files against their schemas
python tools/validate_configs.py --all

# Print the effective runtime config (post-merge of defaults + overrides)
python tools/print_effective_config.py
```

The majority of anomalous braking behavior in testing traces back to incorrect `μ` seed values or a wrong `TPI_THRESHOLD`.

### 4.2 Layer 1 — Log & Telemetry Triage

All runtime events are structured JSON logs. Use the log parser to isolate the relevant window:

```bash
python tools/log_parser.py \
  --input logs/run_<timestamp>.jsonl \
  --start "2026-08-12T10:00:00" \
  --end   "2026-08-12T10:01:00" \
  --level WARNING
```

Key fields to examine:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tpi` | Real-time threat index; values near threshold are suspect |
| `mu_estimate` | Kalman-filtered friction; sudden drops indicate sensor noise |
| `a_cmd` | Commanded deceleration; compare to `a_actual` for actuator lag |
| `pipeline_latency_ms` | Should remain below `latency_spec_ms` from constraints doc |

### 4.3 Layer 2 — Unit & Integration Test Isolation

Run the failing scenario in the simulation harness to reproduce deterministically:

```bash
# Reproduce a specific log scenario
pytest tests/simulation/ -k "test_wet_road_high_speed" -v

# Run with increased verbosity and physics trace
pytest tests/simulation/ --log-cli-level=DEBUG --physics-trace
```

If a test is flaky, check the random seed in `tests/conftest.py` and fix it for deterministic reproduction.

### 4.4 Layer 3 — Algorithmic Inspection

Use the interactive notebook to inspect the model at a specific timestep:

```bash
jupyter lab notebooks/debug_session.ipynb
```

The notebook provides:
- Step-by-step TPI calculation trace
- Kalman filter state visualization
- Side-by-side comparison of predicted vs. actual stopping distance

### 4.5 Layer 4 — Hardware & Embedded Debugging

Only escalate here after Layers 0–3 are cleared.

```bash
# Capture CAN bus trace for 30 seconds
python tools/can_capture.py --duration 30 --output logs/can_trace.asc

# Decode and diff against expected signal timeline
python tools/can_diff.py --trace logs/can_trace.asc --expected docs/hardware/expected_signals.yaml
```

**Golden rule:** Never modify embedded firmware without a corresponding unit test that exercises the changed signal path.

### 4.6 Debugging Escalation Matrix

| Symptom | Start At | Likely Cause |
|---|---|---|
| False positive braking (no hazard) | Layer 0 | `TPI_THRESHOLD` too low or `w_trajectory` misconfigured |
| Late braking (hazard missed) | Layer 1 | Sensor fusion latency spike or `d_margin` too small |
| Oscillating brake command | Layer 3 | Kalman filter divergence; check process noise matrix Q |
| Brake actuator not responding | Layer 4 | CAN message ID mismatch or timing violation |
| High latency warnings in logs | Layer 2 | Scheduler preemption; check real-time thread priority |

---

## 5. AI Tool Workflow

AI coding assistants are used as **accelerators, not autopilots**. Every AI-generated code block must be reviewed against the algorithm design document before merge.

### 5.1 Task Allocation by Tool

| Tool | Best Used For | Avoid Using For |
|---|---|---|
| **Cursor** | In-editor refactoring, multi-file context edits, quick fixes | Safety-critical algorithm logic (review required) |
| **GitHub Copilot** | Boilerplate generation, test scaffolding, docstring completion | Final PR approval decisions |
| **Gemini** | Research, architecture trade-off analysis, long-context document synthesis | Real-time embedded code generation |
| **Microsoft Copilot** | Documentation drafting, requirements summarization, stakeholder comms | Low-level C/Python debugging |

### 5.2 Prompting Standards

When prompting any AI tool for code in this repo:

1. **Always supply the constraint document** as context (paste `docs/architecture/constraints.md` or reference it).
2. **Specify the safety margin** explicitly: *"Assume μ_min = 0.2, a_max = −8.5 m/s²."*
3. **Request tests alongside code** in the same prompt.
4. **Ask for a brief rationale** of any algorithmic choice before accepting.

### 5.3 Review Gate

All AI-generated code must pass:

- [ ] Automated CI pipeline (lint → type-check → unit tests → integration tests)
- [ ] Manual review against `docs/architecture/algorithm_design.md`
- [ ] Safety-critical path sign-off (if touching `src/core/` or `src/middleware/`)

---

## 6. Repo Conventions

### 6.1 Branch Naming

```
<type>/<short-description>

Types: feature | fix | docs | refactor | perf | test | chore

Examples:
  feature/kalman-friction-estimator
  fix/can-message-timeout
  docs/update-workflow-guide
  perf/reduce-pipeline-latency
```

### 6.2 Commit Message Format

Follow **Conventional Commits**:

```
<type>(<scope>): <short summary>

<body — optional, wrap at 72 chars>

<footer — optional: BREAKING CHANGE or issue refs>

Examples:
  feat(core): add trajectory overlap weighting to TPI
  fix(middleware): correct CAN message byte order for brake cmd
  docs(guide): add Phase 3 integration checklist
  test(simulation): add wet-road edge-case scenarios
```

### 6.3 Pull Request Checklist

Every PR must have:

- [ ] Linked issue number in the PR description
- [ ] All CI checks green
- [ ] At least one reviewer approval (two for `src/core/` changes)
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` entry under `[Unreleased]`
- [ ] No TODO comments left untracked (open an issue instead)

### 6.4 Versioning

This project follows **Semantic Versioning (SemVer)**:

```
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH

MAJOR — breaking API or safety-model change
MINOR — new feature, backward-compatible
PATCH — bug fix or documentation update
```

Tags are created on `main` only after a full release review.

### 6.5 Directory Conventions

```
.
├── config/             # Runtime configuration YAML files
├── docs/               # All documentation (architecture, hardware, ops, safety)
├── notebooks/          # Jupyter notebooks (exploration & debug; NOT production code)
├── src/
│   ├── core/           # Algorithm implementation — highest review bar
│   ├── middleware/      # Sensor fusion, CAN interface, scheduler
│   └── ml/             # ML models and inference wrappers
├── tests/
│   ├── unit/           # Pure function tests, no hardware
│   ├── integration/    # Tests requiring hardware rig or full stack
│   ├── simulation/     # Physics simulation scenarios
│   ├── hil/            # Hardware-in-the-loop tests
│   ├── fault_injection/ # Adversarial / edge-case tests
│   ├── regression/     # Baseline suite run on every release
│   └── smoke/          # Post-deployment sanity checks
└── tools/              # Developer CLI utilities (log parser, config validator)
```

---

## 7. Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **TPI** | Threat Priority Index — composite score ranking detected hazards |
| **d_horizon** | Forward-looking distance within which threats trigger braking |
| **μ (mu)** | Road-surface friction coefficient, estimated via sensor fusion |
| **HIL** | Hardware-in-the-Loop — testing where real hardware replaces simulated components |
| **Kalman Filter** | Recursive optimal estimator used here to fuse noisy friction signals |
| **CAN Bus** | Controller Area Network — vehicle communication protocol |
| **Jerk Limit** | Maximum rate of change of acceleration, enforced to prevent passenger discomfort |
| **TPI_THRESHOLD** | Configurable minimum TPI score required to escalate a threat to the actuator |
| **a_max** | Maximum commanded deceleration (negative value, m/s²) |
| **d_margin** | Fixed safety buffer added beyond the computed stopping distance |
